title: First this, then that
translation: The full moon doesn't stay round for a moment. It starts to wane right away. If you're not paying attention, you probably can't see it change much in one night. An illness getting worse is the same. It never stops, and before you know it death is close.

But while the illness isn't serious yet and death still seems far off, you go on thinking the way you always have, as if things will stay as they are. "First I'll get a lot done in this life. Then I'll settle down and devote myself to the Buddhist path." Then you fall ill and you're at death's door, and you haven't done a single thing you wanted. It's hopeless. You regret all the years you wasted, and you promise yourself: "If I get through this and live, I'll work day and night, and I'll get this done, and that, and never slack off." Then you get worse, you're not yourself any more, and you die in confusion.
That's how it goes, every time. So get this into your head first, and soon.

If you plan to finish what you want first and turn to the path when you have time, the wants will never end. Life is an illusion. What are you going to get done in it? All your wishes are delusions. When a wish comes into your mind, know that it's your confused mind talking, and don't act on any of them. Drop everything right now and turn to the path. Then nothing is in your way, there's nothing you have to do, and body and mind are at peace for good.

literal: The roundness of the full moon does not abide even for a moment, and soon wanes.
To a person who pays no attention, perhaps it does not seem to change so much within one night.
An illness growing heavier, too, has no interval in which it abides, and the time of death is already near.

But while the illness is not yet acute and one is not heading towards death, used to thinking of things as permanent and ordinary, one thinks, 'After accomplishing many things in life, I will quietly practise the Way', and meanwhile

one receives an illness, and when one faces the gate of death, not one wish has been accomplished, there is nothing to be said, one regrets the laziness of the years and months, and one probably makes a vow, 'If this time I recover and keep my life, I will join night to day and accomplish this thing and that thing without slacking', but soon, as it grows heavier, one loses oneself in confusion and dies.
There are surely only people of this kind.
Everyone should first, quickly, set this in their mind.
If one intends to turn to the Way after accomplishing one's wishes and having leisure, the wishes will never be exhausted.
In a life that is like an illusion, what would one accomplish?
All wishes, without exception, are delusion.
If a wish comes to the mind, know that the deluded mind is confused, and do not do even one thing.
When one at once casts off all things and turns to the Way, there are no obstacles, nothing to be done, and body and mind are at peace for long.

notes.text: {住|ぢう}す: 'to abide, to stay as it is', a Buddhist word (the edition gives the reading ぢう). Nothing abides: the moon begins to wane as soon as it is full. Compare the moon in section 83.

notes.quote: 常住平生の念にならひて
notes.text: {常住|じやうぢう}: 'permanent, always there'; {平生|へいぜい}: 'everyday'. Thinking that things will go on as they are is the basic mistake, in Buddhist teaching: nothing is permanent.
{道|みち}: here the Buddhist path, practice aimed at rebirth in paradise or enlightenment. {修|しゆ}す: 'to practise'. The translation says 'the Buddhist path' once and then 'the path'.
{懈怠|けだい}: 'laziness', especially about religious practice (modern reading also けたい). The edition gives the reading けだい.
'Joining night to day': working without a break. Modern Japanese still says {夜|よ}を{日|ひ}に{継|つ}いで.

notes.quote: この類のみこそあらめ
notes.text: 'There will only be this kind': everyone does it. こそ … め: the realis form of む.
{如幻|によげん}: 'like an illusion', a stock Buddhist image for life, which looks real but has no substance (the edition gives the reading によげん).
{妄想|まうざう}: in Buddhism, any thinking that comes from delusion. The edition reads it まうざう, the Buddhist reading; modern {妄想|もうそう} means 'a fantasy, a delusion' in the psychological sense.
{放下|はうげ}: 'to throw away, to let go of everything', a Buddhist word (compare section 112). The same demand, drop everything now, runs through sections 59 and 188.
{所作|しよさ}: 'what one does, a task'. Modern {所作|しよさ} means 'manners, movements'. Here: nothing left that you have to do.
